title: How to Ask Your Credit Card Company for a Lower APR: Call Script
meta_description: How to ask your credit card company for a lower APR: a word-for-word call script, what to say if they say no, a call log template and a plan B.
quick_answer: To ask your credit card company for a lower APR, call the number on the back of your card, ask for account services and say: “I’ve been a customer for [X] years and always pay on time. I’d like to request a lower APR. What can you do?” Then pause. Mention only real competing offers. A cut isn’t guaranteed, so log the call and have a backup plan.
key_takeaways: Before you call, write down your current APR, your balance, your on-time payment record and any real competing offers.
Make one clear request for a lower APR. Then stop talking and let the agent answer.
If the answer is no, ask what would help you qualify, ask for a note on your account and try again in a few months.
Before you accept a hardship program or a temporary rate, get three things in writing: how long it lasts, what rate comes after and how it's reported to the credit bureaus.
Log every call (date, agent, reference number and offer), then check your next statement for the new rate.
No luck? Compare the avalanche method, nonprofit credit counseling and a balance transfer.
who_this_is_for: This guide is for anyone carrying a credit card balance who wants to pay less interest by asking their card company for a lower APR and wants a clear plan if the answer is no.
intro: Asking your credit card company for a lower APR takes one phone call and costs nothing but your time. APR (annual percentage rate) is the yearly interest rate charged on any balance you don't pay in full by the due date. Even a modest cut means less interest while you pay the balance down. This guide gives you a word-for-word script and exact replies for the three most common outcomes: a flat no, a hardship program offer or a temporary rate. You'll also get a call log template and a clear plan B. A lower rate is never guaranteed, but going in prepared gives you the best chance and tells you what to do next either way.

steps.name: Find your numbers
steps.text: Open your latest statement or online account. Write down your purchase APR, balance and minimum payment. To see what a cut is worth, estimate your monthly interest as balance × APR ÷ 12.

steps.name: Review your payment history
steps.text: Count how many months in a row you've paid on time and how many years you've had the card. If you've had a late payment, prepare a one-sentence explanation of what has changed since.

steps.name: Gather real competing offers
steps.text: Collect any balance transfer or low-rate card offers you've actually received. For each one, note how long the promotional rate lasts, the transfer fee and the rate after the promotion ends.

steps.name: Set your goal and backup plan
steps.text: Decide what you'll ask for and what you'll do if the answer is no. Your backup could be the avalanche method, nonprofit credit counseling or a balance transfer.

steps.name: Call the official number
steps.text: Use the customer service number on the back of your card or on your statement. Ask for account services or the team that reviews interest rates.

steps.name: Make one clear request
steps.text: Use the script in this guide. Mention your on-time payments and how long you've been a customer, ask for a lower APR, then pause and let the agent respond.

steps.name: Handle the response
steps.text: If the answer is no, ask what would help you qualify and ask them to note your request on the account. If you're offered a hardship program or a temporary rate, ask how long it lasts, what rate it goes back to and how it's reported before you accept.

steps.name: Log and confirm
steps.text: Write down the agent's name, the reference number and the exact offer. Ask for written confirmation, then check that the new APR shows up on your next one or two statements.

steps.name: Move to plan B if needed
steps.text: If the rate doesn't change, compare the avalanche method, a nonprofit credit counselor and a balance transfer. Use the break-even check in this guide before applying for any new card.

sections.heading: How to Prepare Before You Call
paragraphs: To prepare, gather four facts before you dial: your current APR, your balance, your payment history and any real competing offers. With these in front of you, you can make a specific, believable request instead of a vague one.

Start with your latest statement or online account. Many cards charge separate APRs for purchases, balance transfers and cash advances, so note which rate applies to the balance you're carrying. In the US, most card APRs are variable. That means an index, such as the prime rate, plus a margin set by the card company. A permanent cut usually means a smaller margin, so your rate can still move when the index changes.

Your on-time payment record is your strongest argument. Count how many months in a row you've paid at least the minimum by the due date, and how long you've had the card. If you had a recent late payment, prepare a one-sentence explanation and say what has changed since.

Next, work out what a cut is worth. A rough estimate of monthly interest is your balance × APR ÷ 12. Here's a made-up example: a $4,000 balance at 24% APR costs about $80 a month in interest at first, while 18% would cost about $60. That's a saving of roughly $20 a month at the start, and knowing the figure keeps you focused on what matters.

Timing helps too. Good moments to call include after a long run of on-time payments, after your credit has improved or soon after you've received a genuine competing offer. If you can wait, avoid calling right after a missed payment. Decide on your backup plan now so you don't feel pressured into a deal you don't fully understand.
bullets: The card's name and the last four digits of the account number
Your current purchase APR, plus any other APRs on the account
Your balance, minimum payment and the date of your last payment
How many months in a row you've paid on time and how many years you've been a customer
Any real competing offers: how long the promotion lasts, the transfer fee and the rate afterward
Your monthly payoff budget and your backup plan

sections.heading: How to Ask Your Credit Card Company for a Lower APR: Word-for-Word Script
paragraphs: The most effective script is short. Say who you are, confirm your current rate, make one clear request backed by your payment record, then stop talking and let the agent answer.

Call the customer service number on the back of your card or on your statement. Never use a number from an unexpected email, text or call. At the phone menu, ask for account services. If the first agent says they can't change rates, politely ask to be transferred to the team that can. Some card companies call it account review or customer retention.

Fill in the brackets below and read the lines as written. Keep your tone friendly and factual. Front-line agents often have limited authority, and a calm, specific request is easier for them to approve or pass to someone who can.

If your card company offers secure messaging or in-app chat, you can send a written version instead: “I’ve had my [card name] account for [X] years and have paid on time for [X] months. I’m paying down my balance and would like to request a lower purchase APR. Could you review my account, tell me what you can offer and let me know whether a review involves a credit check?” Save a copy of the message for your call log.
bullets: Opening: “Hi, my name is [Name]. I’m calling about my [card name] account ending in [last four digits].”
Confirm the facts: “Before we start, could you confirm my current purchase APR and balance?”

The ask: “I’ve been a cardholder for [X] years and I’ve paid on time for the last [X] months. I’m working to pay down about [$amount], and the current rate makes that harder. I’d like to request a lower APR. What can you do for me?” Then pause.

If you have a real competing offer: “I’ve received a balance transfer offer with a [X]-month promotional rate. I’d prefer to stay with you and pay this down here, but I need a lower rate to make that work.”

If they say yes: “Thank you. Before I accept, does this involve a credit check? What’s the new APR? Does it cover my current balance and new purchases? When does it start, and is it permanent or temporary?”
To close: “Could you send written confirmation? And may I have your name or agent ID and a reference number for this call?”

sections.heading: What to Say When the Agent Says No
paragraphs: When the agent says no, ask what would change the answer, ask them to note your request on the account and end the call politely. A first no isn't always the final word.

Card companies decide based on their own policies, your credit profile, your history with the account and interest rates in general, and they can simply decline. A supervisor or account review team may have options a front-line agent doesn't, so asking once to be transferred is reasonable. Use the lines below to find out more, not to apply pressure.

Don't threaten to close the account unless you're truly prepared to do it. Closing a card doesn't erase what you owe. It also lowers your total available credit, which can raise your credit utilization (the share of your available credit you're using). Many credit scoring models take utilization into account.
If you try again, use the same facts and log each call. If several attempts over a few months don't work, move on to the plan B options below.
bullets: Ask for someone else: “I understand. Is there a supervisor or account review team that could look at my rate?”
Find out the requirements: “What would I need to do to qualify for a lower rate in the future?”
Ask for alternatives: “Are there other options, like a promotional rate on my current balance or a fixed payment plan?”
Leave a record: “Could you note on my account that I asked for a rate review today?”
End politely: “Thanks for checking. I’ll review my options and may call back.”

sections.heading: What to Say if They Offer a Hardship Program
paragraphs: A hardship program is a plan run by your card company for customers in financial difficulty. It may temporarily lower your APR, reduce your minimum payment or waive some fees. Terms vary widely, so get the details before you agree.

Agents may suggest one if you mention job loss, lower income, illness or a similar setback. Only describe a hardship you're actually going through. Common trade-offs include a frozen or closed card, relief that ends after a set period and a note on your account.

You don't have to decide on the spot. Ask whether the offer will still be there if you call back in a day or two. A program that closes the card can still be worth it if it saves you a lot of interest. Just weigh that against having less available credit.
bullets: “What exactly changes: the APR, the minimum payment, the fees or all three?”
“How long does the program last, and what rate and payment apply when it ends?”
“Can I still use the card while I’m enrolled, or will it be frozen or closed?”
“How is this reported to the credit bureaus?”
“Are there any fees or paperwork, or do I need proof of hardship?”
“Can you send me the full terms in writing before I accept?”

sections.heading: What to Say if They Offer a Temporary Rate
paragraphs: A temporary rate is a lower APR for a set number of months. It only helps if you know when it ends, what rate it goes back to and which balances it covers.

Then do the math. Divide your balance by the number of months in the offer. That shows roughly what you'd need to pay each month to clear the balance before the rate goes back up. Here's a made-up example: a $3,000 balance with a 12-month lower rate needs about $250 a month, plus whatever interest the lower rate still charges.
Set a calendar reminder for about a month before the offer ends. That gives you time to check your progress, ask about an extension or line up another option.
bullets: “How many months does the lower rate last, and what exact APR applies afterward?”
“Does it apply to my current balance, new purchases or both?”
“Could anything end it early, like a late payment?”
“Is there a fee to sign up, and does accepting it involve a credit check?”
“Will I get the terms in writing?”

sections.heading: Call Log Template and How to Confirm the New Rate
paragraphs: A call log is a simple written record of every conversation with your card company. It's your evidence if a promised rate never shows up on your statement.

Copy the fields below into a notebook, spreadsheet or notes app, and fill in one entry per call. Record only the last four digits of your card, and never store passwords or full account numbers in your log.

After any agreed change, check your next one or two statements for the new APR. If it's missing, call back and give the date, agent name and reference number from your log. If that doesn't fix it, use the card company's formal complaints process. If you still need help after that, contact your regulator or ombudsman, such as the CFPB in the US or the Financial Ombudsman Service in the UK.
bullets: Date and time, the number you called and the department you reached
Agent's name or ID and the reference or case number
APR and balance before the call
What you asked for
What they offered: new rate, how long it lasts, conditions and fees
Your decision: accepted, declined or still thinking
Start and end dates of any new rate
Written confirmation received (yes or no, and the date)
Follow-up date and next step

sections.heading: What to Do Next If the Answer Is No
paragraphs: If your card company won't lower your APR, there are three common next steps: the avalanche method, nonprofit credit counseling or a balance transfer. Each one suits a different situation.

With the avalanche method, you pay the minimum on every card and put every extra dollar toward the card with the highest APR. When that card is paid off, add its payment to the card with the next-highest rate. Paying the most expensive debt first usually means paying the least interest overall. The downside is that the first card can take a while to clear if its balance is large.

A nonprofit credit counselor can review your budget and, if it fits, set up a debt management plan. Under a typical plan, the agency asks your card companies for lower rates or waived fees, and you make one monthly payment to the agency. Plans often last several years, the cards in the plan are usually closed and there may be setup or monthly fees, so get all costs in writing. In the US, look for agencies affiliated with the National Foundation for Credit Counseling (NFCC) or the Financial Counseling Association of America (FCAA). Elsewhere, check your government's money advice service. Don't confuse credit counseling with debt settlement, which works differently and carries bigger risks to your credit.

A balance transfer moves your balance to a new card with a lower promotional rate. Expect a transfer fee, usually a percentage of the amount you move, and a hard credit inquiry when you apply. Card companies generally won't let you transfer a balance between two of their own cards. Any balance left when the promotion ends is charged the card's regular rate.

To check the break-even point, compare the transfer fee with the interest you'd otherwise pay. Here's a made-up example: a 3% fee on a $4,000 balance is $120. The transfer may come out ahead if two things are true: your current card would charge more than $120 in interest over the time you need to pay off the balance, and you can realistically clear it before the promotion ends.
bullets: The avalanche method fits if you can pay more than the minimums and want to keep your cards open.
Credit counseling fits if you're struggling to cover the minimums on several cards.
A balance transfer fits if your credit is in good shape and you have a realistic plan to pay off the balance during the promotion.

sections.heading: Risks, Limits and Common Mistakes to Avoid
paragraphs: Asking for a lower APR carries little risk, but there's no guarantee it will work, and a lower rate won't clear your debt on its own.

Treat the call as one tool in your payoff plan, not the whole plan. This guide is general information, not personal financial advice. For decisions about your own situation, consider talking to a nonprofit credit counselor or a licensed financial adviser.
bullets: Keep paying extra after a rate cut. A lower APR reduces your interest, not your balance.
Don't keep adding new purchases to the card you're trying to pay down.
Don't exaggerate competing offers, your income or a hardship. Be accurate in everything you tell the card company.
Don't accept a deal you haven't had fully explained, especially one that closes the card or ends after a few months.
Watch out for unexpected callers offering to lower your rate. Hang up and call your card company yourself, using the number on your card.
Consumer credit rules differ by country. Check with your regulator, such as the CFPB in the US or the FCA in the UK, to see which rules apply to you.

recommendations.not_for: Anyone happy with a notebook or spreadsheet. You don't need a new app to log a few calls. Whatever tool you use, never store full card numbers, passwords or security answers in it.

faq.question: Does asking for a lower APR hurt your credit score?
faq.answer: Usually not. Asking for a lower rate on a card you already have typically doesn't involve a hard credit inquiry, but policies vary, so ask the agent before you accept any change. Hardship programs or closing the card can affect your credit in other ways, so ask how any change will be reported.

faq.question: How often can you ask your credit card company for a lower APR?
faq.answer: There's no universal rule. If you're turned down, a sensible approach is to wait a few months, keep paying on time and ask again once your payment record or credit has improved. You can also ask the agent whether there's a waiting period before your rate can be reviewed again.

faq.question: How much lower should I ask my APR to be?
faq.answer: There's no standard amount. A practical approach is to ask an open question, such as “What can you do?”, then compare the offer with your current rate and any real competing offers. If you want to name a number, base it on a genuine offer you've received, not a figure you've read online.

faq.question: Should I threaten to close my account to get a lower rate?
faq.answer: Only mention closing the account if you'd actually do it. Closing a card doesn't erase the balance, and it lowers your available credit, which can raise your credit utilization. A polite request plus openness to other options usually leaves more possibilities open.

faq.question: Can I get a lower APR if I've missed payments?
faq.answer: You can still ask, but expect it to be harder. If a penalty APR was added after a late payment, ask what you need to do to get your standard rate back and when the account will be reviewed. Some countries have rules that require card companies to review penalty rates after a period of on-time payments, so check your cardholder agreement or your regulator's website.

faq.question: Can I ask for a lower APR online instead of calling?
faq.answer: Some card companies accept requests by secure message or in-app chat, but options vary. A phone call is usually easier when you need to ask follow-up questions. If you write instead, use the short template in the script section and save a copy of the conversation in your call log.

conclusion: Asking your credit card company for a lower APR costs nothing but a phone call and can cut the interest you pay. Prepare your numbers, use the script, ask clear questions about any hardship program or temporary rate and log every call. A yes isn't guaranteed, so go in with a backup plan: the avalanche method, nonprofit credit counseling or a balance transfer that passes the break-even check above. Whatever the answer, real progress comes from paying the balance down steadily. Consumer credit rules differ by country, so check with your local regulator or a licensed adviser for decisions about your own situation.
